clinicalPearls: The omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct normally connects the embryonic midgut to the yolk sac and involutes in early gestation; incomplete obliteration yields a spectrum of remnants.

Meckel diverticulum is by far the commonest remnant, arising when the intestinal end persists; a patent duct, umbilical sinus, vitelline cyst, umbilical polyp, or fibrous band represent other patterns.
A completely patent duct presents in the neonate with enteric or faecal discharge from the umbilicus, whereas a persisting fibrous band predisposes to volvulus and internal herniation.
An umbilical polyp is a firm, bright-red mucosal nodule of retained gastrointestinal epithelium that does not respond to silver nitrate, unlike an umbilical granuloma.
A vitelline cyst forms when both ends of the duct obliterate but a central patent segment traps secretions.
Ectopic gastric mucosa within a remnant can ulcerate and bleed, and a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan helps localise it.
Persistent umbilical discharge demands distinction from a urachal remnant, which drains urine rather than enteric content.
Symptomatic remnants and persistent bands are managed by surgical excision, including division of the band to prevent obstruction.
reference.pathophysiology: During early development the omphalomesenteric duct links the yolk sac to the primitive midgut and normally regresses as the placenta takes over nutrition. Failure of this involution leaves a remnant whose clinical form depends on which portion persists and whether it remains patent. Persistence of the intestinal end produces a Meckel diverticulum; a fully patent lumen creates an entero-umbilical fistula; obliteration of the ends with a patent centre yields a vitelline cyst; and a fibrous cord may persist as a band tethering the bowel to the umbilicus. Retained mucosa is frequently gastrointestinal and may include ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue, whose acid secretion causes ulceration and bleeding. A persistent band or the mesodiverticular vessels provide a fixed point around which small bowel can twist, producing volvulus or internal herniation.
additionalDifferentials: patent vitellointestinal fistula versus enterocutaneous fistula
additionalInvestigations: sinogram or fistulogram to define a patent tract
technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy for ectopic gastric mucosa
contrast luminal studies to demonstrate communication with bowel
MRI for complex or ambiguous anatomy
redFlags: bilious vomiting or obstruction suggesting volvulus around a persistent band
gastrointestinal or umbilical bleeding indicating ectopic gastric mucosa
persistent enteric or faecal umbilical discharge
signs of peritonitis from perforation or strangulation
prolapse of bowel mucosa through a patent duct
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent after complete excision of the remnant. Untreated persistent bands carry an ongoing risk of obstruction, and unrecognised ectopic mucosa may bleed.
pitfalls: confusing a vitelline remnant with a urachal anomaly by not distinguishing enteric from urinary discharge
treating an umbilical polyp as a granuloma with repeated silver nitrate application
overlooking ectopic gastric mucosa as a source of occult bleeding
failing to divide an asymptomatic band discovered incidentally, leaving a future obstruction risk
incomplete excision leaving residual mucosa at the umbilicus
